messages.subject: Discussion on R-help of Google code standards for R
messages.subject_clean: Discussion on R-help of Google code standards for R
messages.body_plain:
Even if you don't regularly read the R-help mailing list you may want
to check the discussion on the R Coding Standards suggested at
Google.  The discussion thread can be seen at

http://www.nabble.com/Google%27s-R-Style-Guide-td25189544.html

and the style guide itself is

http://google-styleguide.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/google-r-style.html

Naturally the discussion degenerates into S3 versus S4 classes and
methods, which is the R equivalent of the vi-vs.-emacs or perl-vs-
python-vs-ruby flame wars on other lists.

messages.subject: R flashmob
messages.body_plain:
Dear Madison R users,

Hello from a U-W Madison graduate!

We're organizing an "R Flashmob" to get
students and researchers asking and answering R questions on the very useful
questions site "stackoverflow.com <http://stackoverflow.com>" during one fun-filled hour.

We were wondering if you might help out in promoting this
event by blogging something about it and/or emailing it to students or
researchers who would benefit by having a friendly, efficient resource for
asking and answering R questions. It would be great if you could!

An easily-forwarded invitation is below.

Thanks on behalf of the R Flashmob #2 organizers,

Dan Goldstein

Michael E. Driscoll

JD Long

(Also at http://www.decisionsciencenews.com/?p=1042
)

>From: The R Flashmob Project

>Subject: R Flashmob #2

>

>You are invited to take part in R Flashmob, the
project that makes the

>world a better place by posting helpful questions and
answers about the

>R statistical language to the programmer’s Q & A
site stackoverflow.com <http://stackoverflow.com>

>

>Please forward this to other people you know who
might like to join.

>

>FAQ

>

>Q. Why would I want to join an inexplicable R mob?

>

>A. Tons of other people are doing it.

>

>Q. Why else?

>

>A. Stackoverflow was built specifically for handling
programming questions.

>It’s a better mousetrap. It offers search (and is
well indexed by search engines),

>tagging, voting, the ability to choose the “best”
answer to a question, and the ability to

>edit questions and answers as technology progresses.
It has a karma system to

>reward people who are happy to help and discourage
MLJs (mailing list jerks).

>

>Q. Do the organizers of this MOB have any commercial
interest in stackoverflow?

>

A. None at all. We’re just convinced it is the best way
to help and promote R. All

>the content submitted to stackoverflow is protected
by a Creative Commons

>CC-Wiki License, meaning anyone is free to copy,
distribute, transmit, and

>remix the information on stackoverflow. All the
content on stackoverflow is

>regularly made available for download by the public.

>

>INSTRUCTIONS – R MOB #2

>Location: stackoverflow.com <http://stackoverflow.com>

>Start Date: Tuesday, September 8th, 2009

>Start Time:

>10:04 AM – US Pacific

>11:04 AM – US Mountain

>12:04 PM – Madison, WI

>1:04 PM – US Eastern

>6:04 PM – UK

>7:04 PM – Continental W. Europe

>5:04 AM (Weds) – New Zealand (birthplace of R)

>Duration: 50 minutes

>

>(1) At some point during the day on September 8th,
synchronize your watch to

>http://timeanddate.com/worldclock/personal.html?cities=137,75,64,179,136,37,22

>

>(2) The mob should form at precisely 4 minutes past
the hour and not beforehand.

>

>(3) At 4 minutes past the hour, you should arrive at
stackoverflow.com <http://stackoverflow.com>, log in,

>and post 3 R questions. Be sure to tag the questions
“R”. See the posting

>guidelines at http://stackoverflow.com/faq
to understand what makes a good

>question.

>

>(4) Follow R Flashmob updates at http://twitter.com/rstatsmob

>

>(5) Post twitter messages tagged #rstats and
#rstatsmob during the mob,

>providing links to your questions.

>

>(6) During the R MOB, you can chat with other
participants on the #R channel

>on IRC (freenode). To do this, install the Chatzilla
extension on Firefox.

>Click “freenode” on the main screen. Then type /join
#R in the field at the

>bottom of the screen. Then chat.

>

>(7) If you finish posting your three questions within
the 50 minutes, stick

> around to answer questions and give “up votes” to
good questions and answers.

>

>(8) IMPORTANT: After posting, sign the R Flashmob
guestbook at

>http://bit.ly/6F8B2

>

>(9) Return to what you would otherwise have been
doing. Await

>instructions for R MOB #3.

--

Dan Goldstein | Assistant Professor of Marketing

London Business School S232 | Regent's Park

London NW1 4SA | United Kingdom | +44 20 7000 8611

messages.subject: transform a table?
messages.body_plain:
hello everyone, i'm a molecular biology grad student and found this forum off google. i'm new to R, so i hope you dont mind a fairly basic R question. Thanks in advance for any help or pointers. we're using R to manipulate the results of SQL queries and create an HTML output. I'm starting with a table that looks essentially like this: Name Field1 Field2 John value1 value2 Jane value3 value4 My table is stored as a dataframe. I'd like to efficiently produce an output that iterates through each row, transposes it and outputs an HTML table (one per row). like this: Name: John Field1: value1 Field2: value2 Name: Jane Field1: value3 Field2: value4 I can accomplish this by looping through each row, then outputting that row's table. This gets the job done, but it seems there must be a better way. I'm going to need to do this sort of conversion a lot, so the simpler the better. is there a better way to approach it than the code below? is there a more general term for the sort of transformation i'm trying to make that might help guide my searching? i realize i need to look into better methods of outputting HTML tables (like r2html). here's the basic idea. 'labkey.data' is the data frame produced by my SQL query: D<-labkey.data H<-colnames(D) T<-t(D) L<-length(D$id) output <- "" for(i in 1:L) { R<-my.row <- D[i, ] R<-t(R) Len<-length(R) output <- paste(output, "") for(j in 1:Len) { output <- paste(output,"") } output <- paste(output, "
", H[j],":", R[j], "

") } write(output, file="${htmlout:output}") Thanks for any help.

This gets the job done, but it seems there must be > a better way. I'm going to need to do this sort of conversion a lot, > so the simpler the better. is there a better way to approach it than > the code below? is there a more general term for the sort of > transformation i'm trying to make that might help guide my searching? > > i realize i need to look into better methods of outputting HTML tables > (like r2html). > > here's the basic idea. 'labkey.data' is the data frame produced by my > SQL query: It would help if you created a toy example so those who respond can show the actual code. A couple of comments on your code, using single-letter names as identifiers is not recommended just because there are a number of heavily-used functions that have single letter names. Name conflicts are less of a problem now that packages have name spaces but it is best not to tempt fate. > D<-labkey.data > H<-colnames(D) > T<-t(D) > L<-length(D$id) You have the right idea of taking the data frame and transposing it. During this process all the values will probably be converted to character data, if they are not already character. Columns of a data frame can be heterogeneous but the transpose of a data frame is an array with homogeneous data types. The best thing to do when developing code like this is to use the str() function frequently. So str(labkey.data) # shows the structure of the original data frame str(t(labkey.data)) # shows the structure of the transpose You can work on columns of the transposed table with loops and indices, as shown below, but often it is more effective to write a function that produces the desired result from one column then "apply" the function to the columns. It would look like cfunc <- function(cc) { for (nm in names(cc)) output <- paste(output, "", nm,":", cc[nm], "") } Then you can just apply(t(labkey.data), 2, cfunc)) If you are doing this on large data frames you will probably find it more convenient to write to a connection, rather than accumulating all the output in a character string. See the help page for "file" or "open". > output <- "" > > for(i in 1:L) { > R<-my.row <- D[i, ] > R<-t(R) > Len<-length(R) > > output <- paste(output, "") > for(j in 1:Len) { > output <- paste(output,"") > } > output <- paste(output, "
", H[j],":", R[j], "

") > } > > write(output, file="${htmlout:output}") > > Thanks for any help.

On Thu, Sep 10, 2009 at 8:38 AM, bbimber wrote: > > ok, thanks for the advice. i will post data in the future. your > suggestions on creating/applying a function make sense. > > i have one question though. i believe i understand how to create a > file connection and the table rows to it. however, i'm not sure i > understand why this is more convenient that accumulating the data in > string variable (although it is not less convenient either). is a > file somehow handled more efficiently than a large string? is it > because files allow more manipulations (like iterating by line), than > strings? sorry if this is a dumb question, but i'm trying to be sure > i understand why i'm doing what i'm doing. > > thanks again. Constructions like output <- paste(output, "new stuff") become inefficient in an interpreted language because appending to an existing structure usually means that you need to allocate the new structure, then copy the old value and append the new value. Files, on the other hand, are designed to have contents appended to them and the operating system takes care to do this efficiently. Building structures by iterating and appending is discouraged in R. Compare > sqrts <- numeric(0) > system.time(for (i in 1:100000) sqrts <- c(sqrts, sqrt(i))) user system elapsed 64.136 5.680 69.862 > sqrts <- numeric(100000) > system.time(for (i in seq(along = sqrts)) sqrts[i] <- sqrt(i)) user system elapsed 1.04 0.00 1.04 > system.time(sqrts <- sqrt(1:100000)) user system elapsed 0.008 0.000 0.008 Each of these determines and stores the square roots of the first 100000 integers. The third one takes advantage of the vectorization of arithmetic and mathematic functions and is the fastest. The second one preallocates the storage and updates elements in a loop. It suffers from the overhead of interpretation and looping but does not do any copying. The first is appending to an existing structure in a loop and is by far the slowest because of all the copying entailed. > > > On Sep 10, 8:15 am, Douglas Bates wrote: >> On Wed, Sep 9, 2009 at 7:51 PM, bbimber wrote: >> >> > hello everyone, >> >> > i'm a molecular biology grad student and found this forum off google. >> > i'm new to R, so i hope you dont mind a fairly basic R question. >> > Thanks in advance for any help or pointers. >> >> > we're using R to manipulate the results of SQL queries and create an >> > HTML output. messages.subject: mixed effects analysis in R
messages.body_plain:
I need to analyze a biological experiment where cell cultures are
grown at two different conditions, there are 4 "biological" replicates
of each, and 3-4 "technical" replicates.  Biological replicates are
separate batches of cell culture grown from scratch under the same
condition; technical replicates are repeated measurements on the same
batch of cell culture.  I need to determine if there's a significant
difference between the outcomes of the two growth conditions and how
the differences between the biological replicates compare to the
measurement errors.  Is there an accessible tutorial on how to tackle
this?  I've looked at the MASS book, but I find it too terse and hard
to read for somebody who is not a professional statistician.  Also,
looks like R has at least 2 packages for mixed models: nlme and lme4.
Is there an advantage in using one vs the other?

Thanks.

Yury

> looks like R has at least 2 packages for mixed models: nlme and lme4.

lme4 was created after nlme and reflects more recent developments in
the theory and computational methods so I would recommend that
package.  I co-authored both of those packages and would be happy to
talk with you about fitting models with them if you wish (and if you
are in Madison).

messages.subject: Re: Factor to numeric
messages.body_plain:
Are you sure that the decimal digits were dropped or was it just that
when they were printed there was truncation.  One of the options
settings is "digits" which is 7 when you start R.  If you want to get
numbers printed out to a greater number of significant digits then
change that option as, say

options(digits = 14)

You will likely find that the full numeric precision was retained.

output based off a 1000 sample size where y and x are vectors:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: z$y

Residuals   2      6       3
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

degrees of freedom should equal 1 (k - 1 = 1), yet it is outputting
degrees of freedom of 997!!!  Has anyone had this problem before and/
